bio.en: Brian Balfour is the founder and CEO of Reforge, formerly Head of Growth at HubSpot, who has lived through the rise and fall of every major distribution channel and now predicts a new AI-era distribution platform (likely ChatGPT) will open up within months.
bio.zh: Brian Balfour 是 Reforge 的创始人兼 CEO，曾任 HubSpot 增长负责人。他亲历了每个主要分发渠道的兴衰，现在预言一个 AI 时代的新分发平台（很可能是 ChatGPT）会在几个月内打开。

summary.en: Brian Balfour argues a new distribution platform is emerging from the AI shift and will follow a predictable four-step cycle: market consensus (Step 0), a player identifies a moat (Step 1), the platform opens to third parties with a value exchange (Step 2), then closes to monetize and control (Step 3). He predicts ChatGPT is best positioned because of its lead in retention, engagement, and context/memory, and warns the cycle is shortening—so startups must play early and place a focused bet rather than opting out. He also shares what separates companies winning at AI adoption: hard constraints, exiting 'anchors,' and attacking the slowest part of the system.

turns.zh: 好，所以回到建议，说某人坐在那、和经理聊像“Brian 刚分享了所有这个 mind-blowing 建议。我们得挑我们的战斗、我们得挑我们的平台，”你对他们决定把注下哪的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Balfour
turns.en: I think this is a great question because, once again, put my personal prediction aside for a second, and I would encourage everybody to think about it from first principles from who their audience is, what their product is, what stage of company they're at, their current strengths and weaknesses, you got to take all this into account, but if I had to boil it down to a few criteria, the main things I would think about is, when you're looking at new distribution channels and new platforms to choose on, one, going back to what we said before is the better signal is retention and depth of engagement of the users on this platform than it is pure user level like MAU or some other number of signups, one of those vanity metrics. Look at that number one. (00:57:51): Number two is, there's some element of user quality and ability to monetize the users on this platform. I think the starkest example here would be iOS and Android. Even today it's something like Android has 70-some percent of devices, but only 30% of the market share by dollars, and it's the exact flip for iOS. It goes back to what we were talking about earlier, which was, if you bet on Android only, you probably lost, but if you bet on iOS only, even though smaller user base, you were still able to parlay that into a win later. (00:58:31): The third thing to look at is, as these platforms emerge, just analyze what the value exchange is. What are they giving you to incentivize you to develop on their platform? All these platforms, it's a bit of a game of whoever understands the rules and how to arbitrage the rules the best tend to be the ones with the edge and figure that out. (00:58:58): And then finally, fourth on my criteria would be pure scale. Obviously, even if you have those other three, but there's a 200x difference in scale and momentum, obviously you probably have to choose the bigger platform. (00:59:20): But last but not least is as you go through these criteria, these are how you think through entering the game. Once you enter the game, then you immediately need to move to starting to think about how do you exit the game. Knowing once again that that last step is going to come at some point in the future, that there's going to be some closure for monetization, then that's where you have to start thinking through your strategy to exit. (00:59:47): That comes down to things like, okay, well how are you going to own an important part of the user experience or workflow? Or how are you going to accumulate specialized data in context that the major platforms don't have? Or how do you create different types of micro network effects? All of these types of things. So just once again, there is the entrance criteria, but once you figure that out and you feel like you're in the game, you immediately need to move towards, okay, what's my exit plan here, knowing this is all coming.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是好问题，因为再次，把我的个人预测放一边一会，而我会鼓励每个人从第一性原理想：他们受众是谁、他们产品是什么、他们在公司什么阶段、他们当前强弱，你得把所有这个考虑进去，但如果我得 boil 它 down 成几个标准，我会想的主事是：当你看新分发渠道和新平台去选，一，回到我们之前说的，更好的信号是这平台上用户的留存和互动深度、而非纯用户级像 MAU 或某些别的注册数、那些虚荣指标之一。看那个数字一。(00:57:51) 二是，有某种用户质量的元素、和在这平台变现用户的能力。我觉得这里最鲜明例子是 iOS 和 Android。即使今天像是 Android 有 70 几% 设备，但只有 30% 市场份额按美元，而 iOS 正好 flip。回到我们早聊的，也就是如果你只赌 Android，你大概输了，但如果你只赌 iOS，即使更小用户基，你仍能把它 parlay 成后来的赢。(00:58:31) 第三件看的是：当这些平台出现，就分析价值交换是什么。他们给你什么来激励你在他们平台开发？所有这些平台，是个有点谁理解规则、并最好套利规则的游戏，那些往往是有优势并搞清楚那个的人。(00:58:58) 然后最后，我标准的第四是纯规模。显然，即使你有那其他三，但规模和有 200x 差，显然你大概得选更大的平台。(00:59:20) 但最后但非最不重要的是：当你过这些标准，这些是你怎么想进入游戏的。一旦你进游戏，你立刻需要移到开始想你怎么 exit 游戏。知道再次那最后一步会在未来某点来，会有某种为变现的关闭，那才是你得开始想通你的退出策略的地方。(00:59:47) 那落到像：好，那你打算拥有用户体验或工作流的重要部分吗？或你打算累积平台没有的专门数据和上下文吗？或你打算创造不同类型的微网络效应？所有那些类型。所以再次，有进入标准，但一旦你搞清楚、你感觉你在游戏里，你立刻需要朝“好，我这里的退出计划是什么”移，知道这一切在来。

turns.speaker: Brian Balfour
turns.en: Just to quickly explain that transition so it makes sense for people, which is, I started Reforge just with the interest that there was all these incredible leaders out there growing on the front lines of some of the fastest growing companies and they have all this amazing knowledge and I wanted to encode it in useful and practical ways for others. That took the form of courses and content and product, all that kind of stuff at the beginning. Along the way, everybody kept asking us to essentially build the tools to implement what we taught. Because with anything, you can learn as much as you want. You can listen to my podcast, your podcast, Lenny, whatever, as much as you want, but if you don't actually put it into action and implement it, then it's not really going to create value. (01:05:56): People kept asking us to really close that gap and we said no for the longest time. And then about a couple of years ago when AI really started to inflect, it really created this moment that, oh, wow, now there's this opportunity not just to encode this knowledge into content, but also into the products, the software, the tools that we use ourselves. So we started to take a really big bet on that and started to develop this new platform for AI-native product teams. (01:06:22): The first product we launched is called Reforge Insights, which acts like your AI product researcher, aggregates all the feedback from all the sources, uses AI to analyze it, helps you explore it, but also will start to identify what are the gaps, the things that you don't have in your feedback today and auto-generate the research to go gather all those new insights, so complete the full cycle. We're going to launch two other major products as part of this platform before the end of the year, but we'll save that for some future episode. (01:06:53): So that's been our journey. We've seen inside companies that are going through this transformation from two perspectives. One is obviously selling in that tools, but the other perspective is, for 10 years, companies have been coming to us to help them try some sort of transformation with our learning product. (01:07:15): Most companies are not coming to us to just throw a bunch of courses in front of, they're trying to solve some big business problem, some transformation. Now that used to be things like, we've got to figure out this growth thing, or I'm going from sales-led to product-led, or I have more project managers and I need to transition to product managers, something like that. There's some business problem, they're going through some transformation and they saw us as part of that transformation and we got to partake in quite a few of those types of transformation. (01:07:50): Now of course, the transformation that everybody's going through is, okay, how do I become more AI-native? How do I adopt this stuff? We've seen a pretty wide spectrum and from both perspectives of how companies are approaching this. I'm sure everybody's seen that AI, we've been calling them the AI manifesto memos from CEOs out there that proclaim, "We are now AI-native," in some grandiose way, but behind the scenes, there's actually some incredibly stark differences in the actual teeth of what backs up those memos and backs up those executive decrees that we should all be AI. (01:08:43): Just to point out a few of them, which is, one is that I think the most impactful thing that you can do is form really hard constraints. There's other parts that's like, okay, you want to communicate this, you want to establish an owner of who's going to drive this, you want to build an incentives and rewards, and you see this all playing out in things like building it into your career ladders, or some people are starting to introduce this as questions into their performance reviews, all those types of pieces. But the thing that is actually moving the needle are the companies that are defining incredibly hard constraints. (01:09:30): One company that we worked with developed this constraint that they benchmarked against other companies of their revenue size and the team sizes for those stages, and they set a benchmark that we will be one-fifth, each of our functions will be one-fifth the size. What that did is it created a constraint that you couldn't hire above that level, and it forced people to essentially find ways to adopt AI and do things to replace that. So that was one. (01:10:01): You've seen these other ones, I can't remember from what company, that might've been Shopify or another, who was like, you are not allowed new headcount until you prove to us that you are not able to accomplish this with AI. That's another hard constraint. But you also see these other constraints on a smaller level, which is executives saying, "I will not do a product review or review a PRD unless it comes with three prototypes." Something like that. That's the hardest one. Those are the biggest constraints. (01:10:33): I think the biggest change that I'm seeing is, and the things that separates out the top few percent making this change and everybody else is essentially making the hardest decisions, and that hardest decision is going to come down to exiting people. In every transformation, what we see is essentially three groups of folks. We call them the catalysts, the people leading the charge, the people who are experimenting, doing this on their own time, all that kind of stuff. (01:11:07): You then have what we call your converts. These are folks that will make the transformation, they will adapt, but they need structure, they need permission, they need a clear outline, they need a clear plan. I don't say this in a negative way, it's just that that's how some people operate. That's where things like all the things that we were talking about before, which was the decree, the permission, the clear budgets, the rewards, all of those types of things. (01:11:37): But then, inevitably you have a certain percentage that are anchors. They're dragging their feet, they're silently creating friction in the background and all those pieces. There's a big difference in how I think companies are treating and thinking about their strategy for those folks. One group is like, ah, we're going to work with them very passively. Others have set a hard deadline. They're either going to make the transformation by X date or we're going to exit folks. (01:12:13): A lot of people look at this as being really harsh. I think a lot of people would think that, especially individuals, but let me explain it from more of a CEO perspective. A lot of these companies are seeing this AI transformation, the ones that are taking it more seriously, as this isn't adopting new tools, this isn't a light change. This is a fundamental culture change of how we operate as a company. You can't have 20, 30%, whatever meaningful number of it is of your company trying to operate in a completely different way, in a completely different culture. (01:12:48): Cultures thrive on density, and that's why there's sometimes the best ones feel like cults. As a result, from that perspective, it's like, hey, for us to be successful, for this to be the best thing for all employees, we all need to be operating around the same culture of principles and stuff. If that's not you anymore, then we're defining a plan to exit it. (01:13:16): I would say that less than 10% of companies we see are taking this hard stance, but I would say they are probably the ones that are farthest along getting the most adoption and are seeing the most results of the ones that are taking those hard stances. There's a bunch of other stuff I could talk about, but that's the high level of what we've seen across a bunch of different companies.
turns.zh: 就快速解释那个转变让它对人们有意义，也就是：我开始 Reforge 只是因为兴趣——有所有这些难以置信的领导者在一些最快增长公司的前线成长，他们有所有这惊人知识，而我想以有用实用的方式把它 encode 给别人。那采取了课程、内容和产品的形式，所有那种一开始。一路上，人人一直叫我们基本去建工具来落地我们教的。因为无论什么，你能学多少都行。你能听我的播客、你的播客、Lenny，whatever，想听多少听多少，但如果你不真把它付诸行动、落地它，那它不真创造价值。(01:05:56) 人们一直叫我们真关掉那个缺口，而我们最长一段时间说 no。然后大概两年前当 AI 真开始 inflect，它真创造了这个时刻：哦哇，现在有这个机会不只是把这知识 encode 进内容，也进产品、软件、我们自用的工具。所以我们开始在那下个大注、开始开发这个新平台给 AI-native 产品团队。(01:06:22) 我们发的第一个产品叫 Reforge Insights，它像你的 AI 产品研究员，聚合所有来源的所有反馈，用 AI 分析它、帮你探索它，但也会开始识别缺口是什么、你今天反馈里没有的东西，并自动生成研究去收集所有那些新洞察，所以完成完整循环。我们会在年底前作为这平台一部分发另外两个主要产品，但那留待未来某期。(01:06:53) 那是我们旅程。我们看到公司内部在经历这个转变，从两个视角。一个显然是卖那些工具，但另一个视角是：10 年来，公司一直来找我们帮他们试某种转变、用我们的学习产品。(01:07:15) 多数公司不是来找我们就扔一堆课程在他们面前，他们是试图解某个大业务问题、某种转变。现在那过去常是像：我们得搞清楚这个增长事、或我从销售驱动转到产品驱动、或我有更多项目经理而我需要转到产品经理，像那种。有个业务问题，他们在经历某种转变、他们视我们为那转变的一部分、而我们参与了很多那种转变。(01:07:50) 现在当然，每个人在经历的转变是：好，我怎么变得更 AI-native？我怎么采用这个？我们看到相当宽的光谱、从两个视角关于公司怎么 approach 这个。我肯定每个人都看到 AI，我们叫它们 CEO 出的 AI 宣言备忘录，宣告“我们现在 AI-native，”以某种宏伟方式，但幕后，实际上有令人震惊的差异在那些备忘录、那些我们全该 AI 的高管法令背后的真牙齿里。(01:08:43) 就指出几个，也就是：一是我觉得你能做的最有影响的事，是形成真硬的约束。有别的部分像：好，你想沟通这个、你想建一个谁会 drive 这个的 owner、你想建激励和奖励，而你看这全在像建进你的职业阶梯里、或有些人开始把这作为问题引入他们的绩效评估、所有那些块。但真在挪动指针的是那些定义难以置信硬约束的公司。(01:09:30) 我们合作的一个公司发展了这约束：他们对照其他他们收入规模和阶段团队规模的公司 benchmark，他们设了个 benchmark：我们会是五分之一，我们每个职能会是五分之一大小。那做的，是创造了个约束你不能雇高于那级，它 forced 人们基本找方式采用 AI、做取代那个的事。所以那是其一。(01:10:01) 你看到这些别的，我不记得哪公司，也许是 Shopify 或另一个，像：在你向我们证明你不能用 AI 完成这个之前，你不允许新 headcount。那是另一个硬约束。但你也在更小层看到这些别约束，也就是高管说：“我不会做产品评审或评审 PRD 除非它带三个原型。”像那种。那是最硬的。那些是最大的约束。(01:10:33) 我觉得我看到的最大变化、以及把这前百分之几做这改变和别人分开的，本质是在做最硬的决定，而那最硬决定会落到退出人。在每个转变，我们看到本质三组人。我们叫他们催化剂（catalysts），领 charge 的人、在实验的人、在自己的时间做这个的人，所有那种。(01:11:07) 然后你有我们叫皈依者（converts）的。这些会做这转变、他们会适应，但他们需要结构、需要许可、需要清晰大纲、需要清晰计划。我不是负面说这个，只是有些人就那么运作。那就是我们之前聊的所有事的地方：法令、许可、清晰预算、奖励，所有那些类型。(01:11:37) 但然后，不可避免地你有某个百分比是锚（anchors）。他们在拖脚、他们在背景默默制造摩擦、所有那些块。关于这些人的策略，公司对待和想的方式有大不同。一组像：啊，我们会非常被动和他们工作。别的设了硬截止。他们要么在 X 日前做这转变、要么我们退出人。(01:12:13) 很多人看这个觉得真 harsh。我觉得很多人会那么想，尤其个人，但让我从更多 CEO 视角解释。很多这些公司看这 AI 转变——那些更认真取的——为这不是采用新工具、这不是轻改变。这是我们作为公司怎么运作的根本文化改变。你不能有 20、30%、whatever 有意义数字的公司试图以完全不同方式、完全不同文化运作。(01:12:48) 文化靠密度繁荣，而那是有时最好的感觉像邪教的原因。结果，从那视角，是像：嘿，为我们成功、为这对所有员工最好，我们全需要围绕同样文化原则运作。如果那不再是你了，那我们在定义计划退出它。(01:13:16) 我会说我们看到少于 10% 的公司取这硬立场，但我会说他们大概是那些在采用上走得最远、看到最多结果的。有堆别的事我能聊，但那是我们在很多不同公司看到的高层。

turns.speaker: Brian Balfour
turns.en: Well, actually, just a couple more points on this topic we should go. There's probably two more things I would say about this. One is that, if you're a CEO listening to this, I would say that most CEOs or most executives are incredibly disconnected from the actual AI adoption taking place inside their companies. I think a lot of executives who have done these decrees and all that kind of stuff think it's happening naturally, but we talked to both groups. We talked to tons of end users and we talked to tons of executives. (01:14:49): The story we hear from the end users, the PMs, the eng, all that kind of stuff that we talk to using all this stuff, one of the main questions we ask them is, if we're talking to somebody who's picked up a prototyping tool, say, "Well, how many other people on the product and design team are using this?" Almost 90% of the time it's like, "Ah, it's me and this one other person," and everybody else hasn't taken it up. So there's a huge disconnect. (01:15:17): We heard one story, and I can't say the name, but it's a company we all know. It's a major tech company, a tech-forward company. CEO's been out there talking about being AI-native. We talked to one of their principal PMs. Person was early to the prototyping tools. This person shared a prototype with the designer, the eng manager. The designer and eng manager escalated it to the VPs. It caused this whole conversation. Month later, it was still stalling out. This PM happened to then attend a happy hour where the CEO was at and approached the CEO and told the CEO about the experiment that they were running with prototyping and stuff, and the CEO was like, "This is fantastic. Where is it at right now?" He was like, "Oh, well, X, Y, Z happened." The CEO had no idea. And then the CEO is like, "Okay, let me take care of it," and then the next day, it happened. (01:16:18): So one is that you have to go to the ground floor on this stuff. Some of the best companies like Shopify and others are measuring actual adoption and usage. They've gone to the extreme on that front to get a bunch of signals and close to the ground. It just goes to show that this is... I don't think we want to talk about going founder mode, but the reality is it's not just about getting into the weeds of your product, but with something this sizable, you got to get into the weeds of the transformation to really understand what's going on and adopt it. That's point number one. (01:16:58): The second point I would say is Fareed, we do this podcast called Unsolicited Feedback, Fareed Mosavat had this great quote on it. He was like, "Look, your output is constrained by the slowest part of your system." That stuck in my head because it's absolutely true. If you think about AI adoption as a system, there's all parts of the system that could be slowing adoption. It might be that people don't feel permission or they don't have the budget or they don't have the knowledge, all these types of things. In a lot of these cases, it's things like IT, legal, procurement are the slowest part of the friction and are setting the pace of all of this output. (01:17:43): You can also see this in just product teams. There's been all this talk about product managers are becoming the new bottleneck because engineers are speeding up. Well, that's because people are speeding up one part of the product system and not the other parts, which makes sense. They adopted all of this tooling for engineers because they're the biggest head count and the most expensive and all that type of stuff, but product is an output of design, PMs, and engineering. The system is there not to produce code, it's to ship product, and shipping product is the function of those three things. (01:18:19): If you just accelerate one part of the system, you're just going to move to the bottleneck to another part and your actual product output, the output of the system doesn't accelerate, either. I think people have to really understand those two things: what is actually happening on the ground floor, and what is the slowest part? What is the thing that is causing the slowest part of the adoption? Just attack them ruthlessly if you're really serious about making this transition.
turns.zh: 好，其实，就这话题还有几点该去。大概还有两件我会说。一是：如果你是听这个的 CEO，我会说多数 CEO 或多数高管和他们公司内实际 AI 采用极其脱节。我觉得很多做了这些法令和所有的高管以为它在自然发生，但我们和两组都聊。我们聊了大量终端用户、我们聊了大量高管。(01:14:49) 我们从终端用户、PM、工程听到的故事，所有我们用所有这些的人，我们问的主问题之一是：如果我们和刚拾起原型工具的人聊，说“好，产品和设计团队还有多少人用这个？”几乎 90% 时间像“啊，就我和另一个人”，别人都没拾起。所以有巨大脱节。(01:15:17) 我们听到一个故事，我不能说名字，但它是一家我们都知道的公司。大科技公司、技术前沿公司。CEO 一直在外面谈 AI-native。我们和他们一个 principal PM 聊。那人早到原型工具。这人分享了个原型给设计师、工程经理。设计师和工程经理 escalate 它给 VP。它造成整个对话。一个月后，还在 stall。这 PM 碰巧然后参加个 happy hour CEO 在、并接近 CEO 告诉 CEO 他们跑的原型实验，CEO 像“这太棒了。它现在在哪？”他像“哦，好，X、Y、Z 发生了。”CEO 完全不知道。然后 CEO 像“好，让我处理，”然后第二天，它发生了。(01:16:18) 所以一是你得去这东西的 ground floor。一些最好的公司像 Shopify 和其他在衡量实际采用和使用。他们在这前面走到极端去拿一堆信号、接近 ground。它只表明：这……我不觉得我们想聊 founder mode，但现实是它不只是进你产品的 weeds，但有这么大体量，你得进转变的 weeds 去真理解在发生什么、并采用它。那是第一点。(01:16:58) 第二点我会说是 Fareed，我们做个播客叫 Unsolicited Feedback，Fareed Mosavat 在那有个好引语。他像“看，你的输出被你系统最慢的部分约束。”那 stuck 我脑里因为它绝对真。如果你把 AI 采用想成系统，有系统的所有部分可能在放缓采用。也许是人们没感觉许可、或他们没预算、或他们没知识，所有那些类型。在很多这些 case，是像 IT、法务、采购是摩擦最慢的部分、并在定所有这些输出的节奏。(01:17:43) 你也能在产品团队看到这个。一直有所有这关于产品经理变成新瓶颈的谈，因为工程师在加速。好，那是因为人们在加速产品系统的一部分而非别的部分，那讲得通。他们为工程师采用了所有这些 tooling 因为他们是最大 head count、最贵、所有那种，但产品是设计、PM 和工程的输出。系统不是产代码，是发产品，而发产品是那三件事的 function。(01:18:19) 如果你只加速系统一部分，你只是把瓶颈移到另一部分、而你实际产品输出、系统的输出也不加速。我觉得人们得真理解这两件事：ground floor 实际在发生什么、和最慢的部分是什么？是什么造成采用最慢的部分？如果你真认真做这转变，就 ruthless 攻击它们。

What that involves is continuously looking for opportunities for them to make even bigger and riskier decisions for themselves as they grow up and you're there as a support to those decisions, but letting them make those decisions on their own so that by the time they're 18, they are a fully independent person able to think through those decisions themselves. (01:26:50): It's just small things like that, but thinking about the time from zero to 18 as this spectrum of independence and being a supporting role in what you're essentially doing is you're trying to move as many decisions, the percentage of decisions you make for them down to zero by the time that they're 18.
